::: {.callout-note}
## Current phase

**The full student-facing course sequence is published. Weeks 1-4 established
the teaching pattern, Week 5 is classroom-ready, and upcoming weeks receive a
final delivery check before use. Quiz 2 now has complete public and private
delivery packages; the common midterm has a confirmed date and still needs its
detailed instrument.**

Last updated: **19 September 2026**
:::

This page tracks the redesign at the level of decisions and teaching materials.
It complements the [instructor preview](instructor-preview.qmd), which explains
the motivation and the kind of feedback being requested.

course materials remain revisable when classroom evidence identifies a clear

## What Has Been Established

- The course remains a mathematical and statistical software course using
  MATLAB and R.
- The [software matrix](resources/software-requirements.qmd) now distinguishes
  reliable required access from personal installation, scaffolded Quarto use,
  and optional tools. MATLAB plus Symbolic Math Toolbox, R plus six named
  packages, one R editor, PDF export, Blackboard, and ZIP handling are the
  supported student workflow. Git/GitHub and paid AI accounts are not required.
- LLM use is treated as a normal part of the environment, with an emphasis on
  verification rather than trust.
- Students must be able to explain, test, and interpret computational results.
- Weeks 1-4 established the weekly pattern now used across the course.
- Week 3 Meeting 2 now distinguishes warning signs from a genuine new-data
  check: students fit the same candidate degrees on one fixed subset and
  compare RMSE on withheld observations. The activity uses plain-language
  fit/check terminology before Weeks 12-13 formalize training and validation.
- Week 4 now has separate detailed instructor scripts for Sessions 1 and 2.
  Each script preserves the complete 75-minute lesson and includes an optional
  three-minute launch plus 15-minute Quiz 1 overlay with explicit cuts, so the
  two sections can take the quiz in different meetings without losing the
  essential checks or exit ticket.
- Every guided MATLAB and R workflow now has an intentionally incomplete
  starter at its original public URL and a separately labeled possible solution
  under a dedicated `solutions/` path. Main lab and week links lead to starters;
  each guided lab ends with direct solution links, and the code library also
  pairs both versions for later comparison. AI-review scripts remain
  deliberately weak critique targets rather than answer keys.
- Labs are formative practice rather than routine graded submissions. Every
  main and AI-review lab now describes what students should have completed and
  retained. Only an explicitly announced Blackboard checkpoint is collected;
  short in-class exit checks remain separate.
- Muhammad Ismail Yunus is identified on the public home, syllabus, and lab
  pages as the course Teaching Assistant. He supports students during class and
  outside class; students arrange outside-class support with him by email.
- The public home and primary navigation address students first. The full
  15-week sequence is published, completed weeks remain available for review,
  and upcoming weeks receive a final delivery check before use.
- Quiz 1 is fixed as an individual 15-minute in-class Blackboard quiz in Week
  4. Its six content blocks each contain two independently scored one-point
  questions: ten multiple-choice and two one-sentence responses. The class
  groups receive different but equivalent forms. Each student may use one A4
  sheet, handwritten by them on both
  sides, but no other reference material. The quiz requires no MATLAB
  execution and now has a public guide plus two equivalent private forms with
  answer rationales, validated QTI 2.1 import packages, and build checks.
- Quiz 2 is fixed for Wednesday, 30 September, and Thursday, 1 October, with
  the section order reversed relative to Quiz 1. It is a 15-minute in-class
  quiz near the beginning of the meeting and covers material through Week 5;
  material first taught in Week 6 is excluded. Its public guide, two equivalent
  private forms, written-response rubrics, validated QTI packages, and
  Blackboard checklist are complete.
- The midterm is fixed for Saturday, 10 October 2026, from 12:00 to 13:30.
  Scheduling it outside regular class hours allows both sections to sit the
  same 90-minute examination simultaneously and preserves both regular Week 7
  class meetings.
- A plain-language glossary and optional recovery checkpoints after Weeks 5,
  10, and 12 provide beginner support without adding required work.
- The student pages now identify Laurent Alain Najman, the instructor email,
  Banner as the official meeting source, Main Campus classes, SAN Campus
  office, and on-demand appointments whose time and location are agreed by
  email. They also publish the approved
  five-minute lateness threshold, Registrar-based absence substitutions, the
  40% compensation ceiling, and the 10%-per-day late-project penalty.
- Week 5 now follows that pattern with exact symbolic computation, domain and
  assumption checks, a fixed-volume tank optimization problem, independent
  numerical verification, and an AI-answer audit. All new scripts pass the
  complete MATLAB validation harness. Two detailed instructor PDFs now provide
  exact wording, slide-to-MATLAB transitions, TA actions, timed student work,
  Blackboard exit questions, and time-loss contingencies. Session 1 integrates
  the seven-minute Quiz 1 follow-up and the Project 1 readiness checkpoint.
  Session 2 uses the released time for a fuller numerical comparison and
  AI-claim repair.
- Week 6 introduces R through familiar MATLAB ideas before asking students to
  edit a supplied `.qmd` report. It includes objects, vectors, data frames,
  logical selection, missingness, `stopifnot`, checked `ggplot2` figures, and an
  AI causal-claim audit. The projects still use Word/Google Docs reports
  exported to PDF; students are not required to author Quarto documents from
  scratch. All new R scripts and the code embedded in the report scaffold pass
  the validation harness.
- Week 7 uses R's built-in `airquality` data so students can focus on `dplyr`
  rather than file import. Each verb is tied to a row or column invariant;
  missing ozone measurements, group denominators, units, and descriptive-only
  conclusions remain visible. The AI activity diagnoses a pipeline that runs
  but answers a nearby question. All three Week 7 R scripts pass the validation
  harness.
- Week 8 uses `ggplot2::diamonds` to separate quantitative and categorical
  variation, investigate covariation and overplotting, inspect nonpositive
  recorded dimensions, and refine marginal comparisons. Students maintain an
  EDA log that separates findings, doubts, limitations, and next questions.
  The AI activity audits a fluent but causal and anomaly-blind plot
  interpretation. All three Week 8 R scripts pass the validation harness.
- Week 9 supplies a small synthetic wide campus-energy CSV so students can
  practice real file paths without finding data. `readr` schemas, two explicit
  missing-value encodings, parsing diagnostics, `pivot_longer`, 6-by-4 row
  accounting, and building-month key uniqueness are checked. The AI activity
  shows that a 24-row result can still lose identifiers, units, and numeric
  types. All three Week 9 R scripts pass the validation harness.
- Week 10 supplies a synthetic building registry and service-event log. It
  makes string normalization rules, ordered-factor levels, time zones,
  timestamp parsing, primary and foreign keys, relationship cardinality, and
  unmatched rows explicit before joining. The AI activity joins events to
  monthly energy on only `building_id`, expanding nine events to 33 rows; the
  repaired building-month join preserves all nine event observations. All
  three Week 10 R scripts pass the validation harness.
- Week 11 reuses the familiar service-event log so that students can focus on
  program structure rather than another import problem. Named pipeline
  checkpoints expose row, key, type, and group-accounting invariants. Four
  small functions illustrate validation and explicit contracts; normal,
  exact-boundary, missing, and invalid inputs are tested. The AI activity shows
  how a plausible refactor can silently change inclusive-boundary,
  missing-value, and function-argument behavior. All three Week 11 R scripts
  pass the validation harness.
- Week 12 returns to the familiar `airquality` data so that students can focus
  on vectorization and iteration rather than import. It distinguishes
  whole-vector work from repeating a checked function across variable names,
  compares `lapply`, typed `vapply`, and a preallocated loop, and requires one
  status row for every requested batch item. The AI activity shows how `NULL`
  can erase failures and mixed return values can coerce numeric results to
  text. Project 2 is introduced without moving modeling content ahead of Week
  13. All three Week 12 R scripts pass the validation harness.
- Week 13 keeps `airquality` so students can focus on model meaning. It makes
  complete-case row accounting explicit, fits a temperature model and an
  additive temperature-plus-wind model, interprets coefficients within units
  and observed ranges, compares training RMSE with a mean baseline on identical
  rows, and treats standardized residuals and Cook's distance as investigation
  flags rather than deletion rules. The AI activity audits causal language,
  extrapolation, R-squared misuse, training/validation confusion, and ignored
  diagnostics. Quiz 4 remains visible in Week 13 while its detailed design is
  deferred. All three Week 13 R scripts pass the validation harness.
- Week 14 applies the same temperature-plus-wind model to the five monthly
  subsets of `airquality`. A named split and checked list retain every fitted
  model, while one aligned table reports sample size, coefficient intervals,
  training error, fit, and diagnostic evidence. A grouped sensitivity analysis
  shows when one difficult observation materially changes a slope and explains
  why lower error after deleting that row is not validation. The AI activity
  audits a fluent ranking that ignores unequal sample sizes, uncertainty,
  diagnostics, row alignment, and performance on new data. All three Week 14 R
  scripts pass the validation harness.
- Week 15 uses a miniature training-and-validation example from the familiar
  `airquality` data to make communication computationally checkable. Students
  generate exact results, one row-aligned prediction per validation
  observation, a captioned figure, and an artifact manifest from one R script;
  read saved files back; reconcile PDF values with declared tolerances; and
  rehearse the Project 2 bundle from a clean session. The AI activity separates
  one supported baseline comparison from causal, universal-accuracy,
  all-seasons, replacement-model, and no-limitation claims. The example adds no
  new Project 2 model or document format. All three Week 15 R scripts pass the
  validation harness.
- The [course-wide audit](instructor-course-audit.qmd) confirms a coherent
  MATLAB-to-R progression, cumulative validation habits, purposeful dataset
  reuse, and technically healthy materials. Its principal workload concern is
  now resolved through the [student workload guide](weeks/workload-guide.qmd),
  while assessment weeks still require calendar decisions.
- The website remains a complete resource bank, but the ordinary student load
  is now explicit: two class meetings, instructor-selected checkpoints from
  one guided main lab, 4-6 core exercises, and a short in-class exit check.
  AI-review labs are embedded or assigned selectively; Lab 4A is extension or
  alternate work.
- Routine website-based practice targets approximately 90-120 minutes outside
  class in an ordinary week, excluding separately announced project and
  examination preparation. Assessment weeks receive a reduced selection when
  an assessment displaces class time.
- The [project milestone map](projects/project-milestones.qmd) fixes the release
  order. Project 1 has a Week 3 preview, Week 4 group package release,
  first-session Week 5 readiness checkpoint, and a final deadline of Thursday,
  24 September 2026, at 9:00 AM UAE time. Project 2 has a Weeks 9-10 preview,
  Week 12 training release,
  post-Week-13 frozen-plan gate, common Week 14 validation release, and Week 15
  completion window.
- Blackboard keeps previews public, group packages restricted to the
  corresponding group, and Project 2 validation closed until the common
  frozen-plan gate. Exact opening and closing times remain deferred.
- The current enrollment is 66 students: 37 in one section and 29 in the other,
  so individual oral project defenses are not a practical default.
- Project teams may contain one, two, or three students. Three is the maximum;
  pairs and one-person teams are allowed. The final number of group-specific
  packages used for release will be determined after team registration.
- Students from either class session may form one project team. Cross-session
  teams use one course-wide identifier, dataset, submission, and grade, while
  students continue attending their registered sessions. Blackboard access
  across the two sessions remains part of the live dry run.
- Project 1 uses MATLAB and Project 2 uses R.
- Each group receives a distinct synthetic building-energy dataset supplied by
  the instructor.
- The private configurable generator now produces 66 MATLAB datasets, 66 R
  training datasets, and 66 withheld validation datasets. All 66 packages pass
  structural, plausibility, distinctness, and comparability checks.
- Beginner-oriented MATLAB and R starters, fixed results schemas, and separate
  Project 2 validation releases are assembled automatically for every group.
- The private MATLAB and R batch checkers each pass all 66 known-good reference
  submissions and produce a one-row-per-group review table.
- Supplied Word templates guide students through both PDF reports without
  requiring Quarto or HTML. The files can also be edited in Google Docs.
- All 198 release ZIPs pass exact allowlist and fingerprint checks. Project 2
  training packages contain no validation outcomes, and representative ZIPs
  pass a local Blackboard-style upload/download extraction rehearsal.
- The complete generator, hidden reference material, withheld validation data,
  solutions, checker evidence, and release packages are backed up in a separate
  private GitHub repository.
- Students submit PDF reports with executable source code and machine-readable
  results; Quarto and HTML are not required.
- Projects are group-assessed. The remaining 80% of the course establishes
  individual competence through quizzes and examinations.
- The public weekly plan now uses this assessment sequence: Quiz 1 in Week 4,
  Quiz 2 in Week 6, the common Saturday midterm after Week 7, Quiz 3 in Week 9,
  and Quiz 4 in Week 13. Quiz 2 and the midterm have confirmed calendar
  placement; Quiz 3 and Quiz 4 remain working markers.
- There is no mandatory individual project examination. A brief verification
  may occur for a small random sample or when submitted evidence requires
  clarification.

## Deferred Design Questions

The following questions remain open. They do not change the confirmed core
architecture, but they block approval of the final calendar and release plan:

1. What should Quizzes 3-4 measure and how should they be delivered? Quiz 2 is
   fully specified; only its live Blackboard rehearsal remains.
2. How should the common 90-minute Saturday midterm combine code reading,
   implementation, and validation?
3. What exact Blackboard opening and closing times should implement the
   approved Project 2 training, frozen-plan, validation, and completion gates?
Projects have no mandatory individual examination. The approved policy permits
only limited random or evidence-triggered verification of submitted work.

The [project pages](projects/index.qmd) now record the agreed MATLAB-to-R
architecture and the remaining implementation decisions.

The 66-candidate-group student project package is validated:

With 66 students and permitted team sizes of one to three, the final roster
contains 33 groups. They are mapped continuously to `group-01` through
`group-33` and to the corresponding validated candidate packages.

The audit, student workload contract, week-relative project milestone map, and
